summary:
Bali stands under Indonesia's national framework, and that framework is where the legal risk sits. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted anywhere in Indonesia, that provision reaches consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Same-sex marriage remains unrecognised for visitors and residents alike.

The island's own environment is materially milder than the statute book. Travel guidance current to March 2026 describes a "live and let live" basis, records no criminal enforcement against foreign tourists, and names Seminyak (Eat Street and Batu Belig), Canggu and Ubud as the areas with the most consistently LGBTQ+-friendly venues. Public displays of affection are advised for all couples as a matter of discretion rather than law. LGBTQ+ travel advisories rate Bali "Exercise Significant Caution," and the Gayborhood guide scores the destination 6.3 out of 10 with a legal score of 2.0, warning that visitors should keep affection quiet despite the tolerant reputation.

Bali has a directly documented death in custody of a trans traveller. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. His mother in Lima was told during a WhatsApp call that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy at national level now treats LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law; commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Bali also hosts a visible trans feminine (transpuan) community, documented in a 2025 peer-reviewed ethnography. The study records real precarity, misrecognition and discrimination alongside organised informal resistance, and rejects a simple victimhood narrative. Visitors should expect a socially tolerant surface operating on custom rather than legal protection.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement of Indonesia's morality provisions extends well beyond Bali and takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level provisions. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors, so onward travel from Bali carries a different and harsher risk profile.

The gap between local custom and codified law is the central comparison for this territory. Travel sources rate the destination as broadly welcoming while assigning it a legal score of 2.0, and one March 2026 guide states that the new Criminal Code adds complexity to an otherwise permissive picture. The October 2025 presidential decree and the vigilante attacks reported in August 2026 indicate that the national trajectory runs against the island's informal tolerance.
localsOnly:
The 2025 ethnographic article in Anthropology of the Middle East, built on four case studies of transpuan communities in Bali, documents how trans feminine residents navigate circumstances marked by both resistance and misrecognition. The study records persistent discrimination beneath the island's tolerant reputation and challenges narrative framings that cast the territory as a refuge, while also challenging a pure victimhood account by showing sustained community agency.

Residents live under the same national penal code effective January 2026, and no domestic relationship recognition of any kind is available: same-sex marriage is not legally recognised anywhere in Indonesia. The LGBTQ+-friendly venue scene is concentrated in Seminyak, Canggu and Ubud, which functions as an informal geography of safety for residents as much as for visitors, and discretion in public affection is the local norm for couples regardless of sex composition.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources conflict on the reach of the new Criminal Code. A March 2026 travel guide states that same-sex relations are not a criminal offence in Bali under Indonesian national law, while the national penal code in force from 2 January 2026 penalises extra-marital sex, which by the absence of same-sex marriage covers consensual same-sex relations. Whether that provision has been used against same-sex couples in Bali is unresolved in this inventory; reporting describes prosecutions as selective rather than systematic.

No sourced material in this inventory covers enforcement of the 2026 code against foreign visitors specifically at Ngurah Rai airport or in Bali's venues, nor entry screening, passport gender marker rules, or access to gender-affirming care on the island. Those items are not sourced here rather than absent.

The 6.3/10 destination rating and 2.0 legal score are a commercial guide's own composite ratings; their weighting and methodology are not stated in the sources. The circumstances of Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla's death remain contested, with the allegation of a beating denied by Indonesian police, and no sourced outcome for any related legal proceedings.
